interviewQuestions.question: What is the time complexity of quicksort?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It depends on the case, so I'd give all three rather than pick one.

- **Best and average: Θ(n log n).** A pivot that splits roughly in half gives log n levels of recursion with linear partitioning work at each level.
- **Worst: Θ(n²).** If the pivot is always the minimum or maximum, each partition peels off one element, recursion depth becomes n, and the work is the triangular sum.

The part worth saying next is *what triggers the worst case*: with a naive first-element or last-element pivot, an **already-sorted array** does it — and sorted input is completely ordinary in practice (timestamps, auto-increment IDs). All-duplicate arrays break naive two-way partitioning the same way.

So real implementations don't use a naive pivot. **Randomized pivot** or **median-of-three** makes the bad case unreachable by an adversary, and three-way partitioning handles duplicates. Java's `Arrays.sort` for primitives uses a dual-pivot quicksort; for objects it uses Timsort instead, because it needs stability and a worst-case guarantee.

If I needed a hard bound rather than the best average speed, I'd reach for heapsort or merge sort at Θ(n log n) in every case, and pay the constant-factor difference.

**Testing:** whether you can name the case, the bound, and the input that triggers it — not just recite a number.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: Hash map operations are O(1) — under what conditions is that not true, and what would you do about it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
O(1) is the **average** case, and it rests on two assumptions: keys spread evenly across buckets, and the load factor stays bounded.

It breaks when:

- **Keys collide heavily.** A poor hash function, or keys with a shared structure (all ending in the same suffix), can funnel entries into one bucket. With chaining that bucket becomes a linked list and lookup becomes **O(n)**.
- **The map resizes.** A single insert that triggers a rehash is O(n). Amortized it's still O(1), but that one call spikes — which matters if you have a latency budget.
- **An attacker picks the keys.** Hash-collision DoS: a crafted request with a few thousand colliding parameter names pins a CPU. That hit essentially every web stack in 2011.

What I'd do: rely on the language's **randomized hash seed** (Python, Java, Node all do this now) so collisions can't be precomputed; keep the load factor around 0.75; and for untrusted keys prefer a structure with a real worst-case bound. Java's HashMap converts a bucket to a red-black tree once it exceeds eight entries, which caps the damage at **O(log n)** instead of O(n) — a good example of engineering the worst case down rather than hoping the average holds.

**Testing:** whether you know O(1) is an expectation with conditions attached, and can name the mitigations.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: When would you deliberately choose an algorithm with a worse average case but a better worst case?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Whenever the cost of a single slow operation is higher than the benefit of many fast ones — which is most latency-sensitive and adversarial settings.

The concrete cases:

- **Tail-latency SLOs.** Averages don't bound p99. If a request fans out to 100 backends and each has a 1% slow path, about 63% of requests hit at least one. I'd take merge sort or heapsort at a guaranteed Θ(n log n) over quicksort's better average.
- **Untrusted input.** If the input comes off the network, the worst case is something an attacker can request on purpose. A guaranteed bound removes the DoS vector.
- **Real-time or safety-critical work.** A missed deadline is a failure, so amortized and average-case structures are usually banned outright — no dynamic arrays that occasionally do an O(n) resize, no hash tables that occasionally rehash.
- **Predictability for capacity planning.** A structure with a tight bound is far easier to provision for than one with a rare 100x spike.

The trade I'm making is explicit: I give up some average throughput to shrink the variance. In a batch pipeline where only total runtime matters, I'd make the opposite call and take quicksort.

**Testing:** whether you connect complexity cases to real operational concerns — tail latency, security, predictability — rather than treating faster-on-average as always better.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Design judgement

interviewQuestions.question: A batch job that normally takes two minutes ran for six hours last night, on a similar volume of data. How would you approach it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Same n, wildly different time, means the job likely moved from its average case to its worst case — so I'd hunt for a change in input **shape**, not size.

What I'd check, in order:

- **Did the data become sorted or clustered?** An upstream change that starts emitting rows ordered by ID or timestamp is enough to push a naive quicksort or an unbalanced BST insert into O(n²). This is the single most common cause.
- **Did duplicates spike?** One tenant generating millions of identical keys collapses two-way partitioning and floods single hash buckets.
- **Did key distribution shift?** New keys that share a prefix or hash to the same bucket turn O(1) lookups into linear scans.
- **Is there an accidental nested loop?** A membership test moved from a set to a list turns O(n) into O(n²) with no other code change.

For evidence I'd take a stack sample or flame graph during the slow run — a worst-case blowup parks the process in one function, which is immediately visible.

The fix is usually to remove the input dependence rather than to special-case the data: randomize the pivot, use a balanced or self-tuning structure, or switch to an algorithm whose bound holds in every case. Otherwise the same incident returns the next time upstream data shifts.

**Testing:** whether you can reason about input shape as a production variable, which is the practical payoff of this whole topic.
